messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: Chen, Q.; Wang, J.; Su, Z.; Tian, L.; Huang, F.; Liu, T.; Graham, N.; Li, G.; Yu, W. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at low concentration improve coagulation efficiency but induce higher membrane fouling in drinking water treatment. Environmental Pollution. 2024;363:125201.

comparability.reason: PFAS-dosed and PFAS-free control experiments were conducted on the same surface water matrix with the same coagulation, sand filtration, and UF operating sequence; PFAS concentration was the primary varied factor, allowing direct comparison of floc size and UF flux decline as functions of PFAS presence and concentration.

endpoints.interpretation: Floc size after coagulation increased when PFOS or PFOA were present at low concentration compared with PFAS-free control, with the greatest increase at 0.1 μg/L PFAS.
endpoints.reported_term: Floc growth / floc size during coagulation

endpoints.interpretation: UF membrane flux declined more in PFAS-dosed surface water than in PFAS-free control, indicating more severe membrane fouling; the strongest flux decline occurred at 0.1 μg/L PFAS.

limitations.statement: Bench-scale tests used one representative surface water source and two PFAS (PFOS and PFOA), so results may not generalize to other water matrices, PFAS species, or full-scale plant operation.

matrix.value: Representative surface water (drinking water source) from Beijing, China, containing natural algae and organic matter; used as raw water for coagulation, simulated sand filtration, and ultrafiltration.

operating_conditions.name: PFAS concentration levels tested
operating_conditions.qualifiers: PFOS and PFOA each dosed separately into surface water at environmentally relevant concentrations.

operating_conditions.name: Coagulant type
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Prepared as 0.1 mol/L PACl stock in deionized water and used as coagulant for bench-scale coagulation tests.

operating_conditions.name: PFAS stock solution concentration
operating_conditions.qualifiers: PFOS and PFOA stock solutions prepared in deionized water at 100 mg/L before dilution into surface water.

operating_conditions.name: Clean-water control condition
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Used as control to compare floc size and UF membrane flux against PFAS-dosed conditions.
operating_conditions.value: Surface water with algae and coagulant but without added PFAS

pfas_scope.value: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) added to surface water at 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L.
Perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) added to surface water at 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L.

quantitative_findings.name: Relative floc size increase at low PFAS concentration
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: At PFAS concentration of 0.1 μg/L (PFOS or PFOA), floc size after coagulation increased by 1.6 times compared with surface water without added PFAS.

quantitative_findings.name: UF membrane flux decline at low PFAS concentration
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: At PFAS concentration of 0.1 μg/L (PFOS or PFOA), UF membrane flux declined more than 10% compared with PFAS-free control solution.

residuals_byproducts.statement: Study focused on floc formation and membrane fouling behavior; it did not report PFAS removal, transformation, or degradation products through the coagulation–filtration–UF train.
Increased membrane fouling in PFAS-dosed conditions was attributed to higher biopolymer (mainly polysaccharide) secretion by algae, rather than direct PFAS accumulation or reaction on the membrane.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale coagulation, simulated sand filtration, and ultrafiltration tests using surface water (drinking water source) from Beijing, China.

treatment.value: Conventional drinking water treatment sequence: coagulation with polyaluminum chloride (PACl), simulated sand filtration, and ultrafiltration (UF); membrane filtration performance also evaluated with a microfiltration (MF) membrane control.

records.citation: Chen, Q.; Wang, J.; Su, Z.; Tian, L.; Huang, F.; Liu, T.; Graham, N.; Li, G.; Yu, W. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at low concentration improve coagulation efficiency but induce higher membrane fouling in drinking water treatment. Environmental Pollution. 2024;363:125201.

comparability.reason: PFAS-exposed algal cultures were directly compared to PFAS-free controls under the same assay conditions (same algal species, buffer, temperature, and probe concentration); PFAS concentration was the primary variable influencing ROS and antioxidant responses.

endpoints.interpretation: PFOS and PFOA exposure at 0.1–10 μg/L increased ROS levels in C. pyrenoidosa cells compared with PFAS-free controls, indicating oxidative stress induced by low-concentration PFAS.
endpoints.reported_term: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) intensity / oxidative stress in algae

endpoints.interpretation: Activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) in algae increased with increasing PFAS concentration, indicating activation of enzymatic antioxidant defenses; at the highest PFOS concentration (10 μg/L), SOD activity decreased, likely due to inhibition by excessive ROS. Glutathione system and lipid peroxidation markers (e.g., MDA) also reflected oxidative damage.
endpoints.reported_term: Antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD and CAT) and glutathione system

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS-induced oxidative stress altered algal cell integrity and biopolymer secretion (mainly polysaccharides), which the authors link to changes in floc size during coagulation and increased membrane fouling in treatment tests.
endpoints.reported_term: Algal cellular damage and biopolymer secretion as mechanism influencing floc formation and membrane fouling

limitations.statement: Algal toxicity and oxidative stress responses were evaluated for only one algal species (C. pyrenoidosa) and for PFOS and PFOA at a limited concentration range, which may not represent broader phytoplankton communities or other PFAS compounds.

matrix.value: Algal cell suspensions (C. pyrenoidosa) prepared from freshwater microalgae collected or cultivated in conditions representative of surface water; cells resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for oxidative stress assays.

operating_conditions.name: PFAS concentration levels tested
operating_conditions.qualifiers: PFOS and PFOA each dosed separately into algal systems at three concentrations matching those used in treatment tests.

operating_conditions.name: Algae species
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Freshwater microalgae used to represent algae in surface water and assess PFAS-induced stress responses.

operating_conditions.name: Buffer for ROS and antioxidant assays
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Algae cells washed and resuspended in 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for ROS measurements and other biochemical assays.

operating_conditions.name: ROS probe concentration
operating_conditions.qualifiers: DCFH-DA probe used at 10 μM in PBS to stain algae cells for ROS fluorescence measurement.

operating_conditions.name: ROS incubation temperature
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Algae cell suspensions with DCFH-DA probe incubated at 37 °C for 1 h before ROS fluorescence measurement.

operating_conditions.name: Clean control condition
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Used as control to calculate ROS ratios and compare antioxidant responses against PFAS-exposed algae.

pfas_scope.value: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) tested at 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L in algal suspensions.
Perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) tested at 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L in algal suspensions.

residuals_byproducts.statement: PFAS exposure led to oxidative damage in algae cells, evidenced by increased ROS, lipid peroxidation (MDA), and changes in antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT) and glutathione system, but no PFAS degradation or transformation products were reported.

Authors propose that PFAS-induced stress responses in algae increase secretion of extracellular biopolymers (mainly polysaccharides), which then modify floc formation and UF membrane fouling in treatment processes.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale laboratory assays on freshwater microalgae (C. pyrenoidosa) exposed to PFOS and PFOA at environmentally relevant concentrations to evaluate oxidative stress and antioxidant responses.

treatment.value: Exposure of freshwater microalgae (C. pyrenoidosa) to PFOS and PFOA at low (environmental) concentrations followed by measurement of reactive oxygen species (ROS), antioxidant enzyme activities, glutathione system, lipid peroxidation, and cellular damage.
